new_statements.quote: [p. 81] The first important feature to remark is that stress is non-phonemic, just as in the other Campan languages. [p. 83] It can be described by saying that, in bi- and trisyllabic words, the stress is on the penultimate, and, in tetrasyllabic words, it is on the antepenultimate; putting it in other words, in tri- and tetrasyllabic words, the stress falls on the second syllable, and, in disyllabic words, on the first syllable. [p. 86] Penta- and hexasyllabic words with no bimoraic syllable show an identical general pattern with a primary stress on the second syllable and a secondary stress on the fourth

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (701 pp., text; the PDF's metadata gives the title "A gramar of Ashéninka (Ucayali-Pajonal)", author Toni Pedrós Caballero, created 2023-02-17; ISBN 978-94-6093-425-4, DOI 10.48273/LOT0640 on the imprint page). Section 2.5 "Stress" runs printed pp. 81-91 = pp. 109-119, as the locator says. All three quoted sentences are present word for word: p. 81 "The first important feature to remark is that stress is non-phonemic, just as in the other Campan languages."; p. 83 (2.5.1) "It can be described by saying that, in bi- and trisyllabic words, the stress is on the penultimate, and, in tetrasyllabic words, it is on the antepenultimate; putting it in other words, in tri- and tetrasyllabic wo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and governed by tendencies rather than strict rules. Default: iambic disyllabic feet from the left with the final syllable extrametrical, so words of 3-6 syllables carry primary stress on the second syllable (disyllables on the first), with a secondary stress on the fourth in 5-6-syllable words. Weight overrides the default: bimoraic syllables (long vowels, diphthongs) are the strongest stress attractors anywhere in the word, even word-finally; (C)VN syllables do not count as heavy; /a/-syllables attract and /i/-syllables repel stress (strongest word-initially). The iambic pattern breaks down in words of seven or more syllables (author's own summary, 2.5.4, pp. 90-91).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: primary on the 2nd syllable and secondary on the 4th in penta-/hexasyllabic words (p. 86); word-final enclitics (demonstratives, conditional =rika, locative =ki, plural =paeni, exclamative =wee) and possessive suffixes -ni/-ti tend to carry a secondary stress (fn. 35, p. 85; p. 91); the counter-expectative enclitic =maita takes its own primary stress, making two phonological words (p. 86). Author notes the primary/secondary distinction is impressionistic (auditory, no Praat), fn. 33 p. 81.
new_statements.exceptions: Bimoraic syllables attract stress even in disyllables and finally (rowáe 'he eats us', otháwinatakàe); words with initial /ɾ/ stress the first syllable (diachronic *iɾ > ɾ with stress kept in place); /a/ in the first syllable attracts stress (hápokana, páminìro); the syllable before 3rd-person object suffixes -ri/-ro attracts stress in long words; /i/-deletion after /ʃ/ and /ʦʰ/ makes the preceding closed syllable stress-attracting; kin terms vary; 19 of 163 sample words had different stress in narrative vs. slow dictation and 8 repeated words varied between tokens (pp. 82-89).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress (phonological word), non-phonemic. Based on 163 polysyllabic words from four narrative/conversation fragments plus the same words in slow dictation during transcription sessions (p. 82). The author explicitly presents the results as tendencies and leaves a full metrical analysis to future research.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes "Ucayali-Pajonal Ashéninka", which the author defines (p. 2) as covering both Ashéninka Pajonal (ISO cjo, Glottolog ashe1273) and South Ucayali Ashéninka (ISO cpy, Glottolog sout3127), grouped in Glottolog under ashe1274; fieldwork was based in Atalaya (Upper Ucayali) and the Gran Pajonal. The stress statement therefore applies to sout3127 jointly with ashe1273. The thesis (p. 81-82) also warns that J. Payne's 1990/1991 "Asheninca stress patterns" probably describes Tambo-Ene Asháninka rather than any Ashéninka variety. Title page prints the defence date as 6 April 2022 while the LOT volume is 2023 (PDF created Feb 2023); cite as 2023.
